paragraphs: The synagogue and the study hall are called a "small sanctuary," as it is written (Ezekiel 11:16), "Yet I have been to them a small sanctuary" - these are the synagogues and the study halls (Megillah 29a). And the halachic authorities wrote that the mitzvah to stand in awe of the Temple applies, by Torah law, to the synagogue and the study hall as well. Therefore one should be careful of their honor and sit there in awe and reverence. And of those who treat them with mockery and levity it is said (Isaiah 1:12), "Who has required this of your hand, to trample My courts?" And the holy Zohar (vol. 2, 131b) spoke at great length of their punishment, and said: whoever converses in the synagogue - meaning, idle and external talk - has no share in "the God of Israel." And we explained the intent in the manner of what Afikei Yehudah, of blessed memory, wrote in his discussion of "Ahab denied the God of Israel" (Sanhedrin 102b): namely, that the Holy One, blessed be He, is called "the God of Israel" because there is no intermediary minister between Him and them, whereas regarding the concealed nations He is called "God of gods," for they have intermediary ministers. And the proof that Israel has no intermediary is that we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, causes His Divine Presence to rest with them in synagogues and study halls. Therefore one who treats them with disrespect appears not to acknowledge that the Divine Presence rests there, and so he has no share in "the God of Israel" - meaning, in this title of "God of Israel" that Israel merited.

clarification.explanation: The synagogue and the study hall are called a "small sanctuary," as it is said, "Yet I have been to them a small sanctuary - these are the synagogues and study halls." The halachic authorities wrote that the obligation to stand in awe of the Temple (by Torah law) applies also to the synagogue and the study hall, and therefore one must be very careful of their honor and sit there in awe and reverence. One who treats them with levity and mockery - it is said of him, "Who has required this of your hand, to trample My courts?" and the holy Zohar spoke at great length of the punishment for this, saying that one who speaks idle words in the synagogue has no share in "the God of Israel." The intent is this: the Holy One, blessed be He, is called specifically "the God of Israel," because there is no intermediary minister between Him and Israel (unlike the nations, who have "intermediary ministers," and so He is called, with respect to them, "God of gods"). The proof that Israel has no intermediary is that the Holy One, blessed be He, causes His Divine Presence to rest literally in their synagogues and study halls. Therefore, one who treats their sanctity with disrespect is as if he does not acknowledge that the Divine Presence rests there, and thereby loses his connection to this special title - "the God of Israel" - that Israel merited.
takeaways: The synagogue and the study hall are a "small sanctuary," and the obligation of awe toward the Temple applies to them by Torah law.
Levity in the synagogue is considered especially severe, since it is tantamount to denying that the Divine Presence rests there.

paragraphs: There are those who converse with children, or converse with one another about matters of livelihood and business - even though these matters are not included among idle talk, it is forbidden to converse about them in the synagogue. See Eshel Avraham, siman 151, se'if 1.

clarification.explanation: Some people are accustomed to converse in the synagogue with children, or to converse with one another about matters of livelihood and commerce. Even though these matters are not mere idle talk (but rather important matters of daily life), it is nevertheless forbidden to speak of them inside the synagogue.
takeaways: It is forbidden to converse in the synagogue even about important matters such as livelihood and commerce, not only idle talk.

paragraphs: One may not eat or drink in them, nor stroll about in them, nor adorn oneself in them, nor enter them because of the sun's heat or because of the rain; and some are stringent even regarding drinking water there, and it is proper to be careful of this wherever possible. However, people who come to the synagogue to study the holy Zohar some hours before Minchah in the summer, when there is great heat and it is impossible to do without water, need not be stringent.

clarification.explanation: One may not eat or drink in the synagogue, nor stroll about in it for no reason, nor adorn oneself in it, nor enter it in order to escape the heat of the sun or the rain. Some are stringent even about drinking water inside it, and it is proper to be careful about this wherever possible. Nevertheless, people who come to study the holy Zohar in the synagogue a few hours before the Minchah prayer during the summer, when the heat is intense and it is impossible to manage without drinking water, need not be stringent in this matter.
takeaways: One may not eat, drink, stroll about, adorn oneself, or enter for shelter from heat or rain in the synagogue.
One who studies the Zohar there in the summer heat may drink water without concern.

paragraphs: One may not make calculations there unless they are for a mitzvah, such as [the accounts of] a charity fund or the redemption of captives. And I wrote in my small book Makbetziel that calculations of taxes - such as reckoning with the tax collectors how much they received and how much they handed over to the government, and likewise [the deliberations of] those who sit to assess the taxpayers so that each one gives according to his wealth - it is not proper to make these calculations in the synagogue or the study hall. Also, a gathering of the community's notables for the repair of civic affairs is best held in a private home, for at such a gathering one can hardly avoid speaking idle and mundane words. And any feast that involves intoxication - even if it is for a mitzvah, such as a siyum on a tractate - is forbidden in the synagogue and the study hall. And in my small book Rav Pe'alim I raised, in a responsum, with the help of Heaven, that it is forbidden to learn the writing and reading of other languages in the synagogue and the study hall, even the Arabic language that we speak and its script; but the Hebrew script, which is a "half-Ashuri" [square] script, is permitted. And there I brought the words of Rav Nachalah LeYisrael and expressed reservations about them.

clarification.explanation: One may not make calculations in the synagogue, unless they are for a mitzvah, such as the accounts of a charity fund or of the redemption of captives. But calculations of taxes - for instance, reckoning with the tax collectors how much they received and how much they handed over to the government, or the deliberations of those who sit to assess the taxpayers so that each one gives according to his wealth - are not fitting to be done in the synagogue or the study hall. Likewise, a gathering of the community's notables for the repair of civic affairs is better held in a private home, since at such a gathering one can hardly avoid speaking idle and mundane words. And any feast that involves intoxication - even if it is for a mitzvah, such as a siyum on a tractate - is forbidden in the synagogue and the study hall. It is further ruled (in the book Rav Pe'alim) that it is forbidden to learn the reading and writing of other languages in the synagogue and the study hall, even the local Arabic language and script - and the same applies to teaching them there; but the Hebrew script (in its semi-Ashuri form) is permitted.
takeaways: Calculations in the synagogue are permitted only for the sake of a mitzvah (charity, redemption of captives); calculations of taxes and public gatherings are not fitting there.
Feasts that involve intoxication are forbidden in the synagogue even when held for the sake of a mitzvah.
One should neither learn nor teach the reading and writing of foreign languages there; the Hebrew script is permitted.

paragraphs: Torah scholars and their students are permitted to eat and drink in the synagogue only in a case of pressing need, but in the study hall they are permitted even without pressing need, and they are permitted to sleep there even a regular sleep. This applies specifically to eating, drinking, and sleeping, but other bodily needs are forbidden. And smoking is included in the category of eating and drinking, which is permitted; but the sexton of the synagogue is forbidden to smoke in the synagogue.

clarification.explanation: Torah scholars and their students may eat and drink in the synagogue only in a case of pressing need, but in the study hall they may eat and drink even without pressing need, and may even sleep there a regular sleep. This permission applies only to eating, drinking, and sleeping - other bodily needs are forbidden there. Smoking is included in the category of "eating and drinking" and is therefore permitted to Torah scholars like the other permitted things; however, the sexton of the synagogue itself is forbidden to smoke in the synagogue.
takeaways: Torah scholars and their students may eat, drink, and sleep in the study hall without pressing need, and in the synagogue only in a case of pressing need.
Smoking is included in the category of eating and drinking, but the sexton himself is forbidden to smoke in the synagogue.

paragraphs: Healthy people who take a walking stick in hand during the rainy season, to help them walk through streets full of mud, should not bring the stick into the synagogue when they come to pray, but should leave it in the place where the sexton sits to hand out prayer shawls to the congregation, near the entrance. But for an elderly or sick person one need not be stringent, and he is permitted to bring his stick in his hand all the way to his actual seat in the synagogue. And behold, here in our town, in the time of the rains, there will be much mud on the shoes, and one should be careful not to enter with a great deal of mud, but should wipe [the shoes] outside.

clarification.explanation: Healthy people who are accustomed to use a walking stick when walking through muddy streets during the rainy season should not bring the stick with them into the synagogue when they come to pray, but should leave it where the sexton sits (near the entrance, where prayer shawls are given out to the congregation). But for an elderly or sick person one need not be stringent, and he is permitted to bring the stick all the way to his actual seat in the synagogue. Likewise, during the rainy days, when shoes become covered with a great deal of mud, one should be careful not to enter the synagogue with a great deal of mud, but should clean the shoes outside first.
takeaways: Healthy people do not bring a walking stick into the synagogue (they leave it with the sexton); the elderly and the sick are permitted to.
Muddy shoes should be cleaned outside the synagogue before entering.

paragraphs: If one needs to enter [the synagogue or study hall] for his own purpose, such as to call someone, he should enter and first recite a psalm or the like from words of Torah, and only afterward call the person he wants. And if he does not know how to read, he should tarry there a little, whether standing or sitting, for this too is a mitzvah, as it is written (Psalms 84:5), "Happy are those who dwell in Your house" - and this "dwelling" refers to tarrying.

clarification.explanation: One who needs to enter the synagogue for a personal purpose, such as to call someone, should enter and first say a chapter of Psalms or some other word of Torah, and only afterward call the friend he is seeking. And if he does not know how to read (or finds it difficult), he should tarry there a little, whether standing or sitting, for this too is considered a mitzvah, as it is said, "Happy are those who dwell in Your house" - and the word "dwelling" here is used in the sense of tarrying.
takeaways: One who enters the synagogue for a personal purpose should first say something from the words of Torah, and only then attend to his business.
Even a brief stay in the synagogue (standing or sitting) is considered a mitzvah.

paragraphs: One may not sleep in the synagogue, even a brief nap; therefore, if one finds his fellow dozing off, he is obligated to wake him - and all the more so if he finds him dozing during the time of prayer, and likewise during the sermon, for by this he turns his ear away from hearing words of Torah, and one sin drags another after it. But for the needs of the synagogue itself, it is permitted to sleep there.

clarification.explanation: One may not sleep in the synagogue, even a passing nap. One who finds his fellow dozing in the synagogue must wake him - and all the more so if he finds him dozing during the time of prayer or during the time of the sermon, for then he turns his ear away from hearing words of Torah, and thus one sin drags another after it. Nevertheless, if the sleep is for the needs of the synagogue itself (for example, to guard it), it is permitted to sleep there.
takeaways: It is forbidden to sleep in the synagogue even for a moment, and one must wake anyone dozing - especially during prayer or a sermon.
Sleeping for the sake of the synagogue itself (such as guarding it) is permitted.

paragraphs: If the synagogue has two entrances, one should not enter by one entrance and leave by the other in order to shorten his way. But if he did not enter in the first place in order to shorten his way, he may leave by the second entrance. And if he entered to pray, it is a mitzvah for him to leave by a different entrance, as it is written (Ezekiel 46:9), "He who enters by the north gate to bow down shall go out by the south gate." And although it is forbidden to enter by one entrance and leave by another in order to shorten one's way, nevertheless, if he is going for the sake of a mitzvah, it is permitted; and likewise, if he entered by one entrance and studied a psalm in the synagogue, he may leave by the second entrance, since he entered for the sake of a mitzvah. However, it is better for him to tarry there a little, so that he will thereby have two mitzvot in hand - study and tarrying.

clarification.explanation: If the synagogue has two entrances, one should not enter by one and leave by the other merely to shorten his way. But if he did not enter in the first place in order to shorten his way (for example, he entered to pray), he may leave by the second entrance. In practice, one who enters to pray - it is a mitzvah for him to leave by a different entrance, alluding to the verse in Ezekiel, "He who enters by the north gate to bow down shall go out by the south gate." Although it is forbidden to enter by one entrance and leave by another merely to shorten one's way, if the walking is for the sake of a mitzvah, it is permitted. Likewise, one who entered by one entrance and studied a chapter of Psalms there may leave by the second entrance, since he entered for the sake of a mitzvah. But it is better for him to tarry there a little, so that he will have two mitzvot in hand - study and tarrying.
takeaways: One should not enter by one entrance and leave by another merely to shorten his way.
One who enters to pray, or to study a word of Torah, it is a mitzvah or permitted for him to leave by the second entrance.

paragraphs: It is a measure of piety not to spit at all in the synagogue, but rather to swallow it into a handkerchief, so that the spittle should not be seen in the air of the synagogue. And if there is some mat or the like spread on the floor there, he should bend down low to the mat and cast it beneath the mat. And if he has neither of these, and was forced to spit on the floor of the synagogue, he should be careful to rub it with his feet; and on Shabbat, when rubbing is forbidden, he should tread on it with his shoe until it is crushed away. And know that, aside from this, a person must be careful everywhere, even when not in the synagogue, not to cast spittle or nasal discharge in front of people, for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Chagigah 5a), "For God shall bring every hidden thing into judgment" (Ecclesiastes 12:14) - this refers to one who spits in front of his fellow and causes his fellow disgust, for he will have to give an account of this in judgment. Therefore, one who sees thick spittle - called "balgam" - coming from phlegm, or nasal discharge, cast upon the floor, it is a mitzvah to cover it with dust or rub it with his shoe and remove it, so that people should not be disgusted, even though it is not his own. See Chesed LaAlafim, siman 90, ot 15. Also, there are people whose nasal discharge is foul-smelling, and therefore the handkerchief with which they wipe it becomes very foul, and its odor rises to those sitting near this handkerchief, causing them great disgust; such people must be careful to change the handkerchief every day, and at the time of wiping should not open the handkerchief before the eyes of onlookers, so that its great filth should not be seen and cause disgust. A person must pay close attention to such matters and be careful about them.

clarification.explanation: It is a measure of piety not to spit at all in the synagogue, but rather to swallow the spittle into a handkerchief, so that it should not be seen in the air of the synagogue. If there is a mat spread on the floor there, one should bend down low to the mat and spit beneath it. If one has neither a handkerchief nor a mat, and was forced to spit on the floor, he should rub the spittle with his feet until it disappears; and on Shabbat, when rubbing is forbidden, he should tread on it with his shoe until it is crushed. In general, everywhere - even outside the synagogue - one must be careful not to spit or clear one's nose in front of other people, for our Rabbis said that "For God shall bring every hidden thing into judgment" also refers to one who spits in front of his fellow and causes him disgust. One who sees thick phlegm - called "balgam" - or nasal discharge cast upon the ground, it is a mitzvah to cover it with dust or rub it away, so that it should not cause people disgust, even though it is not his own. Likewise, one whose nasal discharge is foul-smelling should be careful to change his handkerchief every day, and when using it should not open it in front of onlookers, so that the filth should not be seen and cause disgust.
takeaways: A measure of piety: not to spit at all in the synagogue, but rather to swallow it into a handkerchief or dispose of it discreetly.
In general, one should not spit or clear one's nose in front of people; one should cover or remove phlegm seen on the ground.
Change one's nasal handkerchief every day, and do not open it in front of onlookers.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to slaughter in the synagogue even for the purpose of kaparot, and likewise it is forbidden in the women's section where they pray. But in the courtyard in front of the synagogue, where people do not pray, it is permitted, if it is for the purpose of kaparot; and one who is stringent even there, blessing will come upon him. See Eshel Avraham, siman 151, se'if katan 1. And one who sneezes in the synagogue - one does not say to him "chayim tovim" [may you have a good life]. And one should not kiss his young children in the synagogue, for it is not fitting to display there any love other than the love of the Omnipresent; however, kissing the hand of a Torah scholar is permitted, for this is done in honor of the Torah and out of love for it. And likewise, those who are accustomed that one who is called up to the Torah, upon coming down, kisses the hand of his father or his teacher or other relatives whom he is obligated to honor by Torah law - this too is included in the category of a mitzvah, for he does so in honor of the Name, blessed be He, who commanded their honor. But he should not kiss the hands of relatives whom he is not obligated to honor by law. And likewise, a servant hired by a householder, if he is called up to the Torah, should not kiss the hand of the householder sitting there in the synagogue, for it is not fitting to display honor to flesh and blood in this sanctified place, but only honor of the Omnipresent, blessed be He. And the same law applies if a wealthy man enters the synagogue who is neither elderly nor a Torah scholar: even though people are accustomed to rise before him outside, nevertheless in the synagogue one should not rise before him, for such honor is not honor of Heaven. However, if he is a well-known wealthy man among the leading members of the community, and is particular about this, it is permitted to rise before him for the sake of the ways of peace, for whatever involves the ways of peace is included in the category of a mitzvah; and of this it is said (Pirkei Avot 2:12), "Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven."

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to slaughter in the synagogue, even for the purpose of kaparot, and likewise it is forbidden in the women's section where they pray. But in the courtyard in front of the synagogue, where people do not pray, it is permitted to slaughter there for the purpose of kaparot - and one who is stringent even there, blessing will come upon him. One who sneezes in the synagogue - one does not say to him "chayim tovim." One should not kiss young children in the synagogue, for it is not fitting to display there any love other than love of the Omnipresent; however, kissing the hand of a Torah scholar is permitted, since this is done in honor of the Torah and out of love for it. Likewise, the custom of one who is called up to the Torah to kiss, upon coming down, the hand of his father or his teacher or other relatives whom he is obligated to honor by Torah law - this too is permitted, since he does so in honor of the Name, blessed be He, who commanded their honor. But he should not kiss the hands of relatives whom he is not obligated to honor by law. Likewise, a hired servant, if he is called up to the Torah, should not kiss the hand of his employer sitting there in the synagogue, for it is not fitting to display honor to flesh and blood in this sanctified place, but only honor of the Omnipresent. Likewise, if a wealthy man who is neither elderly nor a Torah scholar enters the synagogue - even though people are accustomed to rise before him outside - in the synagogue one should not rise before him, for such honor is not honor of Heaven; unless he is a well-known wealthy man among the leading members of the community and is particular about this, in which case it is permitted to rise before him for the sake of the ways of peace, since this too is considered a mitzvah - as it is said, "Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven."
takeaways: One may not slaughter in the synagogue or the women's section even for kaparot; it is permitted in the outer courtyard where people do not pray.
One should not kiss young children in the synagogue; it is permitted to kiss the hand of a Torah scholar or a relative one is obligated to honor by Torah law.
One should not rise in the synagogue merely out of honor for a wealthy man, unless it serves the ways of peace.

paragraphs: One should be careful not to pray in the courtyard behind the synagogue, standing behind the wall which the worshippers in the synagogue face, for here one enters into a matter of doubt: some say that one must face the wall of the synagogue, even though this means praying in the opposite direction from the people of that place; and some say that there too one should pray facing the same direction as the people of that place pray. And according to either opinion, one who does the opposite is called "wicked." Therefore one should be careful not to bring himself into such confusion, as mentioned in Chesed LaAlafim, siman 90, ot 4.

clarification.explanation: One should be careful not to pray in the courtyard behind the synagogue, behind the wall that the worshippers in the synagogue face, since here one enters a matter of doubt: some say one must face the wall of the synagogue (even though this means praying in the opposite direction from the people of that place), and some say that there too one should pray in the same direction as the people of that place pray. And according to either opinion, one who does the opposite is called "wicked." Therefore one should be careful not to bring himself into such confusion (Chesed LaAlafim).
takeaways: One should not pray in the courtyard behind the wall of the synagogue - because of doubt as to which direction to face.
There is a dispute whether to face the synagogue's wall or the direction the congregation faces; either way, doing the opposite is called "wicked" - so one should avoid the situation.

paragraphs: If a person has a choice between two synagogues, and in one of them the majority of the congregation prays, it is proper for him to go to the synagogue where the greater number pray, and he should be careful about this at all three prayers - Shacharit, Minchah, and Ma'ariv. And if he has a choice between two synagogues and one of them is farther from his house, when he goes to the farther one he receives reward for his extra steps. Likewise, a synagogue where people pray regularly all year round is more sanctified, and it is good for a person to pray specifically in the more sanctified place. And likewise, a synagogue that has windows facing Jerusalem is more fitting to pray in, and it is good for it to have twelve windows, three on each side - and there is a secret meaning in this matter, as mentioned in Chesed LaAlafim, see there. And our synagogues, which have an open airspace between the bimah and the arks, it is good for a person to pray facing that open space, for there, before beginning the Amidah, he can look up to the heavens and thereby subdue his heart.

clarification.explanation: If a person has a choice of two synagogues, and in one of them the majority of the congregation prays, it is proper for him to go there, and he should be careful about this at all three prayers (Shacharit, Minchah, Ma'ariv). If there are two synagogues and one of them is farther from his house, he receives reward for the extra steps if he goes to the farther one. Likewise, a synagogue where people pray regularly all year round is considered more sanctified - and it is good to pray specifically in the more sanctified place. Likewise, a synagogue with windows facing Jerusalem is more fitting to pray in, and it is desirable for it to have twelve windows (three on each side) - and there is a secret meaning in this. In synagogues that have an open airspace between the bimah and the arks, it is good for a person to pray facing that open space, since there, before beginning the Amidah, he can look up to the heavens and thereby subdue his heart.
takeaways: It is preferable to pray in a synagogue with a larger congregation, even if it is farther away (one receives reward for the extra steps).
A synagogue used regularly all year, with windows facing Jerusalem (ideally twelve), is more sanctified.
It is good to pray facing an open airspace between the bimah and the ark, in order to look up to the heavens before the Amidah.

paragraphs: Regarding the bimah in the middle of the synagogue, where the prayer leader stands, some are meticulous to make it with seven steps, and there is a reason for this according to the mystical tradition mentioned in the holy Zohar. But this is not indispensable, in my opinion; for even if it does not have seven steps, it still has the halachic status of a "bimah" for the purpose of hakafot and for every other purpose - only if it has seven steps is it a mitzvah performed in the most excellent manner.

clarification.explanation: Regarding the bimah in the center of the synagogue, where the prayer leader stands, some are meticulous to build it with seven steps, and there is a reason for this according to the mystical tradition explained in the holy Zohar. But the Ben Ish Chai emphasizes that this is not indispensable: even if the bimah was built without seven steps, it still has the halachic status of a "bimah" for every purpose (such as the hakafot on Simchat Torah and the like); only if it has seven steps is it an additional, more excellent fulfillment of the mitzvah.
takeaways: A bimah with seven steps is an enhancement based on the mystical tradition, but it is not indispensable - even without it, it retains the full halachic status of a bimah.

paragraphs: One may not light an ordinary candle from a candle of the synagogue, and some forbid lighting even a candle for a mitzvah from it, and certainly it is forbidden to read secular matters by its light. And by all opinions, one may not light a cigarette that produces smoke from a candle of the synagogue, and the sextons of the synagogue must be warned about this, for they stumble in this matter. And oil in which a mouse fell and died, which has become repulsive for human consumption, should not be used to light a candle of the synagogue.

clarification.explanation: One may not light an ordinary candle from a candle of the synagogue. Some even forbid lighting a candle for a mitzvah from it, and certainly it is forbidden to read secular matters by its light. By all opinions, one may not light a cigarette from a candle of the synagogue, and the sextons of the synagogue must be warned about this, since they stumble in it. Likewise, oil in which a mouse fell and died (making it repulsive for eating) should not be used to light a candle of the synagogue.
takeaways: One may not light an ordinary candle (and, by all opinions, a cigarette) from a candle of the synagogue.
One should not use repulsive oil (such as oil in which a mouse fell) to light a candle of the synagogue.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to demolish or tear down anything from the synagogue, unless it is done in order to repair and rebuild. Even a single stone may not be torn out of the synagogue or the study hall in a destructive manner; the only permission is when it is done in a constructive manner. And some forbid tearing down the wall of the synagogue in order to make windows for the women's section, since the women's section does not have the sanctity of the synagogue itself, as mentioned in Chochmat Adam, klal 86, ot 15, and see Chayei Adam, klal 17, ot 10. And those who make a large hole in the wall in order to insert pegs on which to place boards, making a kind of shelf on which to put prayer books, tzitzit bags, and the like, do not act properly, since this tearing is not for the sake of the repair and upkeep of the synagogue itself. See Chayei Adam, klal 17, ot 10, and Chesed LaAlafim, siman 151, end of ot 13, and other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to demolish or tear down anything from the synagogue, unless it is done for the purpose of repair and building. Even a single stone may not be torn out of the synagogue or the study hall in a destructive manner - the permission exists only when the purpose is repair. Some forbid even tearing down the wall of the synagogue in order to open windows for the women's section, since the women's section does not have the sanctity of the synagogue itself. Likewise, one who makes a large hole in the wall in order to drive in pegs and place boards on them (as a kind of shelf for placing prayer books, tzitzit bags, and the like) does not act properly, since this tearing is not done for the repair of the synagogue itself but for personal convenience.
takeaways: One may not demolish even a single stone from the synagogue except for actual repair and building.
Making holes in the wall for a personal shelf (for prayer books, etc.) is not considered "repair" and is not permitted.

paragraphs: One whose house is adjacent to the synagogue may make use of the room next to the wall of the synagogue, and it is permitted for him to sleep and to have marital relations in that room. But the wall itself, which separates between the synagogue and the room, one may not use at all, even for a use that is not disgraceful, and it is forbidden to tear even a single stone from the wall, and it is even forbidden to drive in a nail in order to hang something on it. And the community has no authority to grant permission for this, even for payment. But if the wall was built from the outset in partnership between the owner of the room and the synagogue's trustees, then it has the status of an equal partnership, and the owner of the room may make use of his half, but he may not make use of the synagogue's half, even to the extent of driving in a nail. See Ikarei HaD"T, siman 1, ot 14, and Chesed LaAlafim, siman 151, ot 11.

clarification.explanation: One whose house is adjacent to the synagogue may use the room next to the wall of the synagogue, and it is permitted for him to sleep there and to have marital relations in that room. But the wall itself, which separates the synagogue from the room, may not be used at all, even for a use that is not disgraceful, and it is forbidden to tear even a single stone from it, or even to drive in a nail to hang something on it. The community has no authority to permit such use, even for payment. However, if the wall was built from the outset in partnership between the owner of the room and the trustees of the synagogue, then it has the status of an equal partnership - the owner of the room may use his half, but may not use the half belonging to the synagogue, even to the extent of driving in a nail.
takeaways: It is permitted to use a room adjacent to the synagogue (even to sleep there), but it is forbidden to use the dividing wall itself - even to drive in a nail.
If the wall was built in partnership from the outset, it is divided equally, and only the portion belonging to the room may be used.
